clinical_category: Lower respiratory sputum specimen collection - avoiding saliva contamination
blueprint_topic: Accurate collection of diagnostic respiratory specimens to reduce preanalytic error
stem: A nurse instructs a client who can produce sputum for lower-respiratory laboratory testing. Which instruction is appropriate?

options.A: Rinse the mouth with water, then produce sputum from a deep cough directly into the sterile collection container
options.B: Collect saliva from the mouth because oral secretions are equivalent to lower-respiratory sputum
options.C: Use mouthwash immediately before collection and submit the mouth rinse as the specimen
options.D: Touch the inside of the sterile container with the tongue so oral secretions are included with the sputum

rationale: A is correct. Current CDC respiratory-specimen guidance instructs the client to rinse the mouth with water and then expectorate deep-cough sputum directly into a sterile, leak-proof container. CDC also emphasizes distinguishing sputum from oral secretions or saliva; for tuberculosis testing, salivary specimens are unacceptable and good-quality sputum collection is critical. B, C, and D would not follow the recommended lower-respiratory specimen-collection technique and increase the likelihood that the sample reflects oral material rather than the intended sputum specimen.
educational_objective: Collect a quality lower-respiratory sputum specimen by having the client rinse with water and then expectorate deep-cough sputum—not saliva—directly into a sterile container.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Laboratory Testing for MERS — Respiratory Specimen Collection; Tuberculosis Technical Instructions for Panel Physicians
source_version_date: Current CDC MERS laboratory specimen guidance and current CDC tuberculosis technical instructions accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: CDC 'Laboratory Testing for MERS' → Respiratory Specimen Collection → Lower respiratory tract → Sputum: have the patient rinse the mouth with water and then expectorate deep-cough sputum directly into a sterile, leak-proof container. CDC 'Tuberculosis — Technical Instructions for Panel Physicians' → Sputum Collection and Transport: applicants rinse the mouth with purified/distilled water before sputum collection; salivary specimens are unacceptable and collection of a good-quality sputum specimen is critical.
source_claim_supported: Current CDC guidance directly supports mouth rinsing with water followed by deep-cough sputum collection into a sterile container and differentiates acceptable sputum from saliva/oral secretions.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential client-needs subcategory (9–15% of items), within Physiological Integrity; this item tests correct diagnostic-specimen collection to reduce preanalytic error and improve validity of test results.
correction_summary: Substantive rebuild. The source item's inferred mechanism that mouth rinsing specifically reduces oral-flora contamination was replaced with the exact current CDC collection procedure: rinse with water, produce deep-cough sputum, avoid saliva, and collect directly into a sterile container. No unsupported microbiologic mechanism was required for the answer.
audit_findings: The original NCBI Bookshelf root URL did not provide an exact sputum-collection locator.
Current CDC guidance directly instructs water mouth-rinsing followed by deep-cough sputum collection into a sterile container.
CDC separately emphasizes that saliva/oral secretions are not equivalent to a quality sputum specimen.
The final item removes the source rationale's unlocated claim about directly improving culture accuracy through oral-flora reduction and tests the exact collection procedure instead.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct answer, no unsupported timing or specimen-volume rule, no second answer, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
